newsitem.title: ZAIRE: International community moves warily on Zaire plan.
newsitem.headline: International community moves warily on Zaire plan.

text.p: The international community moved warily to assemble an intervention force that could ease the plight starving refugees in eastern Zaire without placing their forces in jeopardy in a battle zone.

Underlining the hazards ahead, fighting erupted on Thursday around the teeming Mugunga refugee camp near rebel-held Goma on Rwanda's border. Armed Hutus among refugees were putting up a last stand against Tutsis.

At the United Nations in New York, the Canadian commander of the force intended to deliver humanitarian aid to eastern Zaire ruled out disarming militia mingling in the refugee camps or separating them from civilians.

At a news conference on Thursday, Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, joined by Canadia's deputy foreign minister, Gordon Smith, said the troops, estimated eventually to exceed 10,000, would not use force unless they were attacked.
U.N. officials said earlier that feeding areas would be set up by the troops and that no armed militia would be allowed to enter. But Baril made no mention of this.

At least 10,000 foreign troops were eventually expected in the region but the initial force would include soldiers from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal, diplomats said. Brazil on Thursday offered 150 troops.
France seemed to be opting for a high-risk deployment of its planned contingent in Zaire that could put it in the midst of Tutsi rebels openly distrustful of the French.
With the United Nations close to giving its final approval the international force, France said on Thursday its troops would secure the airport in rebel-held Bukavu.
The United States said on Thursday it would demand at least an informal ceasefire among factions fighting around Goma before committing troops to a humanitarian aid force in Zaire.

"What we would like is a pledge by the sides that there will be a ceasefire," Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters. But he said that such a "defacto ceasefire" between warring Hutu and Tutsi militia groups would not have to be "a written, signed agreement".

President Bill Clinton on Wednesday tentatively pledged to send about 1,000 U.S. troops to Goma in eastern Zaire and about 3,000 to nearby countries as part of a task force to save more than one million refugees if details could be worked out.
Troop contributing nations and other delegations held a series of meetings with Baril in New York in an effort to define the force's mandate.
Baril said at the news conference that he intended to establish his headquarters for the new humanitarian intervention force in Central Africa in Goma.

"The proposed location of my main headquarters will be in Goma. Of course Goma is partly if not all destroyed and I will have rear elements of my headquarters that will be both in Kigali and Kinshasa," he said.

France, which has led calls for an international mission to help 1.2 million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi uprooted by fighting between Zaire and Tutsi rebels, has said it is ready to send between 1,500 and 2,000 soldiers. They would include 600 paratroopers able to go within 24 hours of U.N. approval.

The United States, still smarting from losses in a peacekeeping mission in Somalia four years ago, agreed grudgingly to join the Both the Americans and the British are moving cautiously, first sending assessment teams to the region.

France, with a history of intervention in Africa and military bases in some of its former African colonies, seemed ready to move. "I hope that by the weekend we'll see the first soldiers on the ground," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told Europe 1 radio.

Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux said later that "France would contribute to ensuring the safety of the platform at Bukavu." Bukavu, near the Rwandan border, has one of the main airports in eastern Zaire as a key staging post for the mission.
Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsis battling the Zaire army and Hutu militias accuse France of backing Hutus who massacred Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994 and then fled en masse to Zaire.
They say a French military intervention in Rwanda that year aided the escape of armed Hutu genocide leaders who are now battling the Tutsi rebels using refugees as a screen.
Some Tutsi spokesmen have openly vowed to fight the French, and rebel leader Laurent Kabila on Thursday repeated rebel demands that states sending troops to Zaire must be "neutral".
France denies charges of bias in the Hutu-Tutsi conflict.
